# The Weight He Carries

Marcus is a 34-year-old man who works as a parole officer in a mid-sized city. He is broad-shouldered and carries himself with a deliberate steadiness at work — the kind of composure that comes from years of managing volatile situations in supervised release offices and on home visits. To his colleagues, he is the calm one, the one who knows how to read a room. What they do not know is that for the past two years, he has been trying to survive something that happened inside what should have been the safest room of all: his own home.

The relationship with Delia began four years ago and, for the first year, felt like something Marcus had been waiting for his whole life. She was sharp and funny, and he was proud to be with her. The violence started gradually — a shove during an argument that he told himself was a one-time thing, a thrown plate he explained away as stress. By the second year, the episodes had escalated. Delia would strike him across the face, dig her nails into his arms, and on one occasion fractured two of his ribs during a confrontation that left him on the kitchen floor, struggling to breathe and too ashamed to call anyone. He did not call the police. He was the one who worked alongside law enforcement. He was the one who supervised men on parole. He told himself, repeatedly, that what was happening to him could not be what it looked like.

He eventually ended the relationship eighteen months ago, after Delia cornered him in the hallway and choked him until he lost consciousness briefly. He left that night and did not go back.

He is now in a new relationship with a woman named Priya, who is patient and gentle. She is the reason he finally agreed to seek help. She noticed that he flinched when she raised her hand to brush his hair back from his forehead. She noticed that he sometimes went somewhere else entirely in the middle of a quiet evening — eyes open but absent, jaw tight, unreachable. He had not told her everything, but enough.

Marcus does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart slamming, certain someone is in the room. He lies still and does a slow inventory of the darkness until his body believes him that he is safe. Sometimes it takes over an hour. At work, he finds himself hypervigilant in ways that go beyond professional caution — scanning the body language of the people he supervises for any sign of sudden movement, positioning himself near exits, rehearsing escape routes. He is good at his job, but it costs him more than it used to.

The intrusions are the hardest part. Without warning, he is back on the kitchen floor, or back in the hallway, the pressure at his throat. A raised voice in the break room, the particular sound of a door slamming, the smell of a certain perfume — any of these can pull him out of the present and drop him somewhere he does not want to be. He has learned to mask the return: a slow breath, a deliberate look at the clock, a neutral expression. He has been masking things for a long time.

What troubles Marcus most, and what he speaks about with visible difficulty, is the shame. He supervises men who have committed serious offenses, and he spent two years unable to stop what was being done to him by someone he loved. He understands, intellectually, that this logic is flawed. He has heard himself say similar things to the people on his caseload. But understanding something and believing it, he says quietly, are two entirely different things. He is still working on the distance between them.
